speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: We have, therefore, embarked on a major transition towards electric vehicles (EVs).

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: As part of this effort, we intend to amend existing legislation in two stages.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: The first stage is the Land Transport Authority of Singapore (Amendment) Bill 2021 tabled before Members today.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: It assigns statutory functions relating to EVs and EV charging infrastructure to the Land Transport Authority (LTA).

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: The second stage involves other legislative measures related to EV chargers that are still being studied.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Possible measures include registration of EV chargers and charger provision requirements for new building and carpark developments.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: MOT is consulting the industry, working through the policy specifics of these measures and will table a separate Bill when ready.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Currently, the regulatory landscape for EV chargers is truncated.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: LTA's regulatory mandate covers road vehicles, including EVs, but it does not cover EV chargers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: The Energy Market Authority (EMA) oversees the regulation of EV chargers which are affixed to the electricity grid.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: The current situation is not optimal because while LTA is in charge of developing the charging infrastructure, it does not have oversight of the regulations governing proper installation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Furthermore, no Government agency oversees the regulation of non-fixed charging solutions like battery swapping.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: We need to change this existing arrangement to better progress adoption of EVs and EV charging technology.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: I am, therefore, introducing the Land Transport Authority of Singapore (Amendment) Bill today to empower LTA with new statutory functions relating to EVs and EV charging infrastructure.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: First, the Bill assigns LTA the function of promoting and regulating the safe use of EVs in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: This squarely charges LTA with the mission to develop and implement EV-related schemes and policies.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Second, the Bill also confers on LTA the function of undertaking or facilitating the development and maintenance of publicly accessible EV charging points and their supporting infrastructure.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: There is clarity now between EMA and LTA in this sphere of work.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Today, all EV chargers must comply with a set of technical standards and safety precautions called the Technical Reference 25, or TR 25.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Previous reviews of TR 25 were administrated by EMA in consultation with other agencies.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: LTA has since taken over from EMA and is currently leading a review of TR 25 with the aim of using the TR 25 to facilitate industry development.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: This Bill formalises LTA's role to lead the TR 25 Review Committee.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Fourth, the Bill makes it LTA's function to cooperate and collaborate with EMA on matters relating to technical standards for fixed EV chargers and the safe use of EV chargers in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Today, EMA enforces TR 25 for fixed EV chargers through regulatory requirements on licensed electrical workers, or LEWs, under the Electricity Act.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Only LEWs are authorised to install fixed EV chargers and they must ensure that the chargers comply with TR 25 before they install them.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Hence, the Bill requires LTA and EMA to work closely together in the regulation of fixed EV chargers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: While LTA sets EV charging standards going forward, EMA will continue to require LEWs to install fixed EV chargers that comply with the latest standards, which will henceforth be set by LTA.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: This Bill provision reflects the close collaboration needed between these two agencies.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: There is therefore a consequential amendment to the Electricity Act to provide EMA with a new statutory function to collaborate with LTA on these matters.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am pleased to note that the amendments are focused on safety and operational capacity, which were among key technical concerns shared during the Budget debates.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I wish to raise four concerns which I hope LTA will look into as they assume their new responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With plans to increase the number of charging points, there are some concerns among residents on safety issues – whether this may lead to situations such as electrical overload and overcharging, resulting in fire outbreaks or worse, an explosion.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There have been several cases of fires and explosions caused by PMDs that were charging overnight, whether domestically or overseas.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, some are asking if similar scenarios could happen with EVs left to charge overnight.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I note that purpose-built EV chargers would be safe but what happens if someone tampers with it or tries to use a non-compatible extension plug, for example?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This brings me to my next point on batteries.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A number of high-profile global recalls were made last year over battery fire risk in EVs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With the recent boom, engineers are in a global race to design the fastest and cheapest EV batteries.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This can result in plenty of revisions along the way, even at the expense of safety.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How will LTA ensure that the winning tenders are committed to adapting continuously to the evolving technology, with safety and quality at top of mind, and how do we ensure that our charging points can be easily adapted as technology progresses?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In Toa Payoh Lorong 8, for example, the EV charging points were built with wires cutting across the pedestrian paths.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This has posed a safety hazard to residents.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This could have been avoided if there had been closer cooperation and consultation prior to this decision.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Clearer guidelines and policies must be spelt out for cross-agency collaboration.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Otherwise, I fear that, in an emergency, time will be wasted in delegating the responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My last point is on national power consumption.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is, in large part, due to EVs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What would the impact of widespread usage of EVs be in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Do we also expect a surge in electricity usage nationwide and will this affect the capacity capabilities of our power stations in the residential areas?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, is there a need to upgrade electricity substations to cope with the potential increase in power usage?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Are they able to cope with the higher usage?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the meantime, there should be more conversations and reassurances on the safety issues related to EVs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Moreover, residents' safety and convenience must not be compromised.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In my Budget debate speech this year, I had raised, among other related issues, the issue of the critical number of charging points required in all residential, commercial carparks and even other public carparks, as well as the design of the carparks vis-à-vis the locations of the charging points as well as my concern that most of the present HDB public and commercial carparks are not being adequately designed to prevent bottlenecks or congestion caused by more than a few cars waiting for the current few charging units available at each carpark, especially as, currently, the lots with the charging units are placed side by side and usually on the lower floors.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Next, beyond the importance of having the right carpark infrastructure or making the necessary conversions or adjustments to ensure the carpark design or infrastructure does not by themselves cause any unnecessary obstruction and inconvenience to motorists and other members of the public during charging, I would also like to ask the Minister whether he will consider any of the following actions to encourage people to move their vehicles away from charging stations immediately after charging so that others are not unnecessarily deprived of their use.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: One, require service providers to impose heavy payments after charging is done if the vehicle is not removed from the station within a short grace period.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Or alternatively, to have carpark authorities impose an escalating fine for motorists continuing to keep the spot occupied after charging and, beyond a short grace period, for example, fines to increase at every 15-minute interval.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Next, I would also like to ask the Minister, for non-landed, private residences and commercial buildings, whether the Government will stipulate a fixed minimum number of charging points in each carpark or what is the ratio of charging points vis-à-vis the number of carpark lots and, if so, for carparks in these non-publicly owned properties as well as public carparks, will the Government stipulate the ratio in any Government regulation.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I hope that the Ministry will look further into this and to provide necessary assistance so that condominiums and their residents will be able to overcome all difficulties arising from the need to obtain adequate general meeting resolution approvals and, in the event of no approvals, to advise them what they should do.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In the meantime, I will also be grateful if the Minister can update us on the Government efforts made so far to ensure that all private condominiums and commercial properties will be able to get adequate support for the installation of charging units beyond the EV Common Charger Grant as well as the adequacy of the grant to all eligible or affected parties.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Tackling the issue of having cleaner energy vehicles on our roads is of great urgency.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The planning and deployment of EVs involve different Government agencies, and a coordinated approach to the design of policies and regulation as well as stakeholder engagement is critical.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Industry players like Borneo Motors and members of the European Chambers' Smart Mobility Committee are all supportive of the Singapore Green Plan 2030 and look forward to collaborating with Government and stakeholders in the eco-system to achieve the goals set.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: For today, allow me to highlight three broad themes which will need further dialogue and consultation amongst the stakeholders and the Government.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The first broad theme is around the EV charging infrastructure.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The first issue around EV charging infrastructure is the choice of standards.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The choice of charging standards will have an island-wide infrastructure impact.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It is good to know that the Government has already identified a TR25 Committee put together such a team to look into this.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Of course, globally, there is a flurry of activities in the industry to come up with the technology that will become the industry standard.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The jury is still out and there is also the related issue of fast charging or slow charging.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The variance between fast and slow charging can range between 20 minutes and seven to eight hours, and the cost of fast charging is estimated to be 30 times the cost of a $10,000 to $12,000 slow charging station.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: How will Singapore decide on the standard to be used?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: How will Singapore manage the risks involved with this big bet depending on how battery technologies advance or if other technologies disrupt, for example, hydrogen?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: A second issue around EV charging infrastructure is the accessibility of chargers which is a key factor affecting the rate of adoption of EVs.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: What is the planned roll-out of these charging points?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Will EV charging be considered a national infrastructure or will the Government leave it to the private sector to decide based on their business models?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: What will be the design point for the charging network, balancing speed, cost, coverage, convenience and load on the grid?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: HDB carparks will be a major real estate for charging points.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: So, will HDB fund the roll-out of the charging infrastructure?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: How does LTA plan to encourage existing condominiums to put in charging stations since MCST will have to fund the capital costs?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Industry players support a more extensive slow-charging network complemented by a fast-charging network for top-up and emergency.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The slow-charging network can be shared or is specific to each EV.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The shared model will require consumer acceptance of some level of inconvenience.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: So, imagine having to drive your EV to a HDB carpark maybe three MRT stations away and then wait for your car to get charged up and then bring it home.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: So, those are the inconveniences that may appear.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The industry is exploring an option for the installation of the slow chargers to be provided as part of the purchase of the EV, similar to how chargers come with our smartphones today.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Does this mean Singapore may need to consider the approach in Japan, where one can buy a car only when one owns a parking lot?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: If that is so, then the EV charging station is individually owned, which also has the benefit of the charging taking place off-peak and not strain the electricity grid.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Is it, however, wasteful since each EV probably only needs to be charged a couple of times a week at most?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The dilemma is how best to balance cost, convenience and social acceptance when deciding between all these options.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: A third issue around EV charging infrastructure is how to handle range anxiety.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: With the average driving distance being 50 kilometres a day, one charge can probably hold up for three to four days.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: That said, access to fast-charging is still needed in the event of "emergencies".

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: In speaking with several mall developers, many are already fitting up a few EV-ready fast-charging stations.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: There are, however, questions around how many lots to provide optimally and the sharing of these lots by EV drivers.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps an intelligent app can help to alert the driver that his or her EV is fully charged and higher parking charges will kick in thereafter if the car is not moved.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: This is but one form of behaviour-changing tactics that could be considered.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Such carrots should help to make fast-charging stations more accessible at malls, office buildings and new developments.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Existing petrol stations and public carparks are also, of course, potential fast-charging sites.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It is exciting that MTI and EDB have attracted Hyundai Motors to set up their electric car manufacturing in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I am sure it will be a highly automated facility but still our Singapore workforce needs to be systematically upskilled to support electrification across all the OEM brands – from manufacturing, service, aftersales – and to ensure that our workers are future-proof.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: There are new opportunities for our workers in this industry as the EV works on digitalisation and there will be new digital jobs in the auto industry.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: We hope that the Skills and Jobs Framework in the new clean energy for the auto industry can be in place early to help current workers upskill and next-gen workers be future-ready.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The industry is ready to collaborate with our IHLs, SSG and WSG.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The third broad theme is around hybrid being the low hanging fruit to decarbonising on our roads.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: While EVs offer the largest reduction in carbon dioxide footprint, drivers could take a while to warm up making their first EV purchase.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I must declare I do drive a hybrid car.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Hybrid presents the lowest hanging fruit to decarbonising our transportation.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Adoption of hybrids is independent of charging infrastructure and the psychological barriers for purchase are significantly lower.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I am told that there are best-in-class hybrid EV powertrains which use a 1.8-litre engine to achieve remarkable carbon dioxide emissions.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: De-carbonising should not come with a premium COE or a premium road tax.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: One other point I would like to bring up is how used cars will be treated.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore is not an early adopter and so there are many best practices and lessons in other cities we can learn from and adapt quickly for our situation.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The industry suggests for the Government to use the many levers at its disposal, namely, car taxes, COE quotas and road taxes, grants, rebates and so on as both sticks and carrots to help accelerate cleaner energy vehicle adoption, both hybrid and EV.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The industry looks forward to participating in MOT and LTA's industry consultation to discuss the above issues, amongst others, and move the agenda into high gear.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Notwithstanding the issues and questions raised, Mr Speaker, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The LTA (Amendment) Bill before us today is brief but significant in marking a milestone in our embrace of EVs as a country.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Electric mobility brings a host of benefits, including lower carbon emissions, lower air pollution and lower noise pollution.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This Bill is thus a step in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: My speech today will raise questions and suggestions relating to our approach towards EVs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The climate emergency rolls on and the Government should move on the EV front with ambition, speed and transparency in setting out regulations and executive actions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Our local conditions are some of the best in the world for an EV roll-out: distances are short, funding is available and we have the capacity in both the Civil Service and private sector to do this.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Battery prices and EVs will only get cheaper with scale and improvements in technology.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The question is how our move to embrace EVs can be made as well-planned, ambitious, fair and sustainable as we can get it.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Before I proceed, I declare my interest as the CEO of a research consultancy that undertakes work in green technology and other sectors.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Private hire and taxi vehicles have much higher utilisation rates than the casual weekend driver, for example.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: To some extent, families with young children are another high usage segment that could use stronger incentives to switch.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The city of Shenzhen in China, for instance, was early to the game in providing direct and indirect subsidies to encourage taxi drivers to go electric.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This encourages network effects, where the industry becomes more willing to install charging and maintenance facilities because the city now has a minimum market of 22,000 EVs via taxis.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Such additional incentives are not without precedent because we already are giving some support to some groups in Singapore for vehicles on the basis that they need to use their vehicles for work, such as in the case of the Disabled Persons Scheme, for example, where exemptions are provided from paying COE and Additional Registration Fee (ARF), provided the vehicle meets certain conditions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Enhancing incentives for high-use drivers to switch to EVs would get us disproportionate traction in achieving our environmental outcomes while buying more time for the development of new public transport infrastructure to attract transitioning drivers of low-utilisation vehicles to switch to EVs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, Mdm Deputy Speaker, we should welcome the reduction in the ARF floor and the revision in the road tax framework, which would come into effect next year for EVs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This is a good first step and will reduce the green premiums EV users have to pay.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This lump sum tax negates some of the savings derived from the reduced ARF but there will probably still be net savings from these measures for EV owners.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, the presence and uncertainty of fuel excise duty rebates makes this cost-benefit calculation for switching to EVs more complicated and less predictable going forward.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The Workers' Party has argued for a phasing in of the fuel duty hike – and I shall not repeat the arguments here – to ensure that our incentives are having the desired effect.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Would the Government consider setting yearly targets for and publicly keep track of EV charging infrastructure – for instance, chargers per car and chargers per region and the corresponding number of EVs on the road?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, Mdm Deputy Speaker, we need more clarity on what the Government's electrification plans are for the Government-owned fleet.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In her reply to my Parliamentary Question in March, Minister Grace Foo said that, "All new purchases for Government-owned fleets will be cleaner and greener where feasible with effect from 2023." I would urge the Government to set clear targets for the electrification of Government-owned vehicles to be in line with the target set for the building of charging infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I would also call on the Government to develop a strategy to nudge motorcycle users towards electric motorcycles as these are also high-use vehicles in many cases as these are heavily used in delivery work.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, Mdm Deputy Speaker, I would like to talk about the e-waste that EVs will generate.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But EV batteries are considered "non-consumer goods" and all producers of batteries are only required to use a licensed waste disposer or e-waste recycling provider.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There does not appear to be any clear mandate to recycle but only rules and responsible handling of end-of-life to prevent illegal dumping and so on.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Such EV batteries are goods that can be leased out and returned to the original producer either through car dealerships or private hire fleet or taxi fleet owners.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It might be cost-effective for these organisations to reuse and recover materials from batteries rather than dispose of them.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We should encourage circularity in our battery production and use.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: My parliamentary colleague, Ms He Ting Ru, will draw attention to the importance of early forward planning and creating an eco-system for e-waste recycling for EV batteries.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This can be married to the support of our locally rooted recycling and material recovery companies in Singapore since Singapore already has businesses that can do this.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, while we push for our EV transition, it is important to note that better low carbon forms of transport, such as public transport and bike riding, are still far better alternatives in terms of emissions and waste, and it behooves us to not lose sight of this fact in any discussion about promoting EVs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Now is the right time to ask if our current public transport goals are ambitious enough.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, the Government has a commendable commitment to doubling cycling paths to 800 kilometres by 2023, with a target of 1,320 kilometres target for 2030.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We should try to frontload our cycling targets in this way, in light of the recent reports of bicycling accidents.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The cycling boom during COVID-19 has created an opportunity to foster a cycling culture for health, recreation and climate benefits.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We should strike while the iron is hot.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Such an expansion of cycling paths should, of course, take into account nature conservation and there should be safeguards to deter cyclists from going off path into nature areas like the Dairy Farm area, for example.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: My parliamentary colleague Mr Dennis Tan has been a passionate advocate for responsible cycling in this House over the years and is an avid cyclist himself.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I urge Members to review the suggestions he has made and continues to make.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: My colleague Ms He Ting Ru will also speak on this theme in her speech on the Bill.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Lastly, Mdm Deputy Speaker, we must be humble and transparent in consultation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: LTA recently said that it was in the midst of an industry consultation regarding private sector participation in public charger deployment.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But can it do more public consultations regarding other aspects of the EV roll-out?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For instance, it can do more to engage those whose COEs are near expiry.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It should also engage members of the public who are about to buy their next car or about to rent a car for private hire driving.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: EVs are an important part of what needs to be done, which makes this debate and this Bill important.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin):    I would like to start by sharing a bit of history.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: About 140 years ago, the first passenger EV invented by the French inventor, Gustave Trouve, was tested on the streets of Paris.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Interest and adoption of EVs grew at that time.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At the peak of their popularity between 1900 and 1912, almost 40% of vehicles in the United States were EVs.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, they began to lose their popularity because of their limited range, lack of electrical power in rural areas, a relatively slower speed and the discovery of large petroleum reserves that made gasoline-powered vehicles cheaper to operate over long distances.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Today, 140 years later, even with improvements in battery and vehicle technology, some of the same concerns still weigh on consumers, such as availability of charging points.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Unlike the 1900s, there are new and pressing environmental concerns that now drive the Singapore Government to encourage EV adoption.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Modern urban transportation needs and the desire for sustainable transportation solutions have made EVs an important strategic solution to deal with these challenges.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am heartened that through this amendment Bill, LTA and EMA are set to collaborate on establishing the necessary policies and frameworks for the EV infrastructure development.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): Mdm Deputy Speaker, the Government has announced the Singapore Green Plan 2030.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These are targets that will spur us towards a cleaner, more sustainable future and help to ensure that our infrastructure is able to meet the anticipated growth of EVs.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am thus heartened that through this amendment Bill, LTA and EMA are set to collaborate on establishing the necessary policies and frameworks for the EV charging infrastructure development.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would, however, like to raise two considerations.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A study of battery fires in EVs showed that the energy and heat released in an EV fire is much higher than petrol or gasoline-run vehicles, indicating a bigger fire hazard and requiring more stringent risk-mitigating efforts.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This point has also been brought up by a fellow Member of the House earlier.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We need to ensure that, in tandem with the rollout of charging infrastructure in public carparks, there would be the need for education, safety precautions and measures, should an accident or electrical mishap occur.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The second is in the design consideration when implementing the charging points.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I understand that these are slow charging points so as not to overload the existing power grid infrastructure.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Earlier, the Minister for Transport has also mentioned that the average electric car has a range of 300 kilometres to 500 kilometres per charge and that the average user may only need to charge his car once every five days, hence, this would spread out the demand for charging points.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, as mentioned by Ms Janet Ang, some studies have shown that some users not only have “range anxiety” but also an emerging phenomenon known as “charging anxiety”.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Charging anxiety arises from drivers' concerns about the charging process, its ease of use and, most importantly, the time it takes to complete the charging.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The duration of the charging process depends on the different charging modes and capacities.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Drivers experience charging anxiety when they reach a charging station without any problem, but then face a long wait to be able to charge because there are not enough charging stations.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some drivers may also want to charge their vehicles to full capacity as often as possible.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When a lot of people are trying to do this, it can create problems: too many cars, not enough chargers.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It would be difficult to try to explain away the driver’s concern in wanting to charge his vehicle often and this will result in possibly long queues and disputes on the use of charging points.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To this, I would like to suggest that LTA study the user journey, charging behaviour and how charging will take place at carparks to optimise the infrastructure design that allows charging points to be accessible to as many parking lots and vehicles as possible and allow for quick flexible installation of additional charging points, if demand increases in a certain area.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: LTA can also consider the feasibility for one or two separate fast charging points powered by, maybe, alternative energy like solar energy and batteries that do not depend on the power grid.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will allow users who want to charge their cars using fast chargers without impacting the existing power infrastructure.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Such technology is currently available and can be considered to complement the current plans.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We need to bring together technology, infrastructure, economic and human behaviour considerations into our planning and policies when implementing the EV charging points infrastructure.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am very glad that we are starting with this amendment Bill.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Notwithstanding my considerations raised, I support the amendment Bill.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Such a move is overdue and is necessary, given the climate emergency we are facing.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: All the measures in this Bill are an appropriate first step.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: There remain key gaps that we must address in order to secure a more sustainable and environmentally-secure future for Singapore.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: My remarks and clarifications today relate to two key areas: first, building an equitable and sustainable EV infrastructure; and, second, stepping up efforts to promote additional green transport alternatives.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The core of the Bill focuses on enabling LTA to promote the use of electric vehicles in Singapore through facilitating the development of and standards for an EV charging infrastructure.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The stellar rise of mobility as a service has given its role more urgency, underlining the importance of having LTA play a role in building up a sustainable mobility eco-system that can minimise the environmental impact of our transport system.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The principle of equitable access to chargers should be enshrined in law.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Yet there are less details about how and where these points would be located.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: What specific payment and funding models are being considered to ensure that the final user will be extended affordable prices?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Would the Government engage residents in deciding the location of charging points and pricing and publicise the results of this engagement?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: What regulations can be put in place to prevent ugly behaviours, such as charger and space hogging, which deprive other users of the chance to charge their vehicles?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Getting out EV support infrastructure right from the very beginning is especially important as the continued growth in mobility-as-a-service means that many drivers and users of mobility devices depend on their vehicles for their livelihoods.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: They conduct deliveries and transport passengers and should be able to continue doing so without having to worry about finding an available charging station to spend 30 minutes or more charging up their vehicle in the middle of their workday.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: EV batteries comprise rare metals that can be hazardous to humans and the environment and are a finite resource that we will soon be in short supply of.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Our EV strategy must consider extending the typical 10-year useful life of the car and have a plan for the electronic waste after that, including adequate facilities to repurpose, recycle and, when there are no other choices, for the safe disposal of such waste.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We need to think ahead about this issue systematically and not scramble when we realise we are being forced to act because of pressing environmental or safety concerns.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: LTA and MOT should coordinate closely with MSE to develop a clear plan.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The public and key stakeholders should also be consulted and must be asked to provide feedback as we prepare our infrastructure to accommodate EVs.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This crucial element should be baked into the system from the start, not patched on in an ad-hoc fashion years down the line.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I also wish to note that EVs are just one component of developing a sustainable transportation eco-system.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The Green Plan 2030 highlighted the importance of continuing efforts to promote an active, healthy lifestyle in Singapore.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This includes promoting cycling and even more eco-friendly means of getting around.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: There is the added benefit of building exercise into our daily commute.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Given on-going trials to repurpose car lanes for pedestrian use and increase bicycle paths, MOT and LTA should use this opportunity to increase adoption of a cycling culture in Singapore.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Preliminary studies have found that bicycle sales have soared in the wake of COVID-19 travel restrictions and lockdowns.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I look forward to the results of LTA's on-going household travel survey to see if there is a marked increase in commuting by bicycle and other more eco-friendly measures.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: If it is, indeed, true that the on-going pandemic has resulted in the uptake of alternative forms of mobility, it would be a shame to let such gains be reversed as we think about moving back to a new normal.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, greener forms of commuting and transport must form an integral part of that new normal from day one.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: To encourage higher ridership rates and more commuting by bicycle, we should introduce legislation to reorient our infrastructure to promote cycling and other low emission options of travel as an alternative means of commuting.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: An obvious place to start will be further amendments to legislation to reorient our infrastructure to promote cycling and other low emission options as an alternative means of commuting and not just as a means of recreation.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I believe that the compact nature of our estate and the large number of residents who cycle in Sengkang, whether for leisure, commuting or as delivery riders, make it a good place to trial our move towards more active travel and mobility options.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The younger population's high reliance on delivery services and proximity to bike networks, such as the Punggol Waterway Park and Sengkang Riverside Park, makes the estate an ideal candidate for a concerted push towards being a truly bike- and pedestrian-friendly town.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Sengkang can and should be a model for how Singapore can move towards sustainable mobility.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We can even go further by considering repurposing car lanes into bike lanes.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is a tried-and-tested approach from cities, such as Taipei, Copenhagen, Amsterdam and Canberra.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: A more considerate road design that embraces bicycles and even PMDs can also address matters of road safety, which is the subject of some of the changes to the RTA Bill that was also debated earlier today.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: If we make it easier for all road users to use pathways and roads safely together, it would naturally engender safer road behaviour.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: To address concerns raised about active mobility options in Singapore's climate, we should also ensure coordination with BCA and other authorities.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Additionally, we could provide additional tax breaks for buildings which provide such facilities by having a green tax relief scheme.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These measures would definitely further encourage active mobility commuting.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We must think ahead and also innovatively to ensure we focus our minds towards fulfilling our commitment to a green Singapore – promoting health and improving transportation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Brief as it may be, it is an important Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It enshrines within LTA’s remit the important duties of promoting, regulating, standardising and otherwise facilitating the use of EVs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have two points of clarification on how LTA will carry out its duties.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first point of clarification is about motorcycles.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Electric motorcycles are better than petrol motorcycles in just about every important way.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They emit far less air pollutants and greenhouse gases than gas-powered motorcycles.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This means less environmental damage and less health problems for riders and pedestrians.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They are also far quieter, something anyone who has lived remotely near a road will appreciate.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These benefits are not lost on our neighbours in Asia.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In Indonesia, the private sector is taking the lead.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Gojek will convert its massive fleet of green "ojeks" or motorcycle taxis into EVs by 2030.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: By contrast, neither the private nor public sector in Singapore has shone a clear light on the future of motorcycles here.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: NEA announced just last month that it will tighten vehicle noise and emission standards for motorcycles.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the same spirit, we can take bolder steps towards adoption of electric motorcycles.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In March 2020, we did take a small step of allowing high-powered electric motorcycles on our roads.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Prices remain high as production has not yet reached a critical mass.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Honda, the world’s largest motorcycle manufacturer, announced just last month plans for four new models of electric motorcycles, three of which will be released by 2024.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Senior Parliamentary Secretary share the Ministry’s plans to address the cost of electric motorcycles?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, will the Ministry consider supporting partnerships between international manufacturers, local dealerships and logistics firms to trial the use of electric motorcycles at low costs?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: SMRT has already taken some steps in this direction.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will the Ministry also consider the EV Early Adoption Incentive to also include electric motorcycles?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will the Senior Parliamentary Secretary share if the 60,000 EV charging points to be built across the island are compatible and convenient for not only electric cars but also electric motorcycles?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Just as important, we must work on a vision.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: On electric cars, taxis and buses, we have spoken loudly; motorcycles need that same clarity.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Senior Parliamentary Secretary share where the Ministry sees motorcycles in 2030 or 2035?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will we aim to keep the same gas-guzzling, smog-spouting models on the road, or will we look to sunset them?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A clear Government vision can steer and accelerate private initiatives.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point is about charging points in condominiums.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This Bill proposes that LTA and EMA’s remit include facilitating the development of accessible charging points.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Ministry share what plans it has to collaborate with EMA and BCA to expand the construction of charging points in condominiums?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A fair proportion of these people likely drive cars, can afford EVs and are more likely to be early adopters.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But they simply will not buy an EV if they cannot get a charging point built where they live.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My colleague Member of Parliament Gan Thiam Poh made a similar point during our Climate Change Motion earlier this year.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Since then, CNA has written an article containing interviews and research, detailing just how difficult and slow the installation of charging points in condominiums has been.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A softer approach is to help condominium AGMs come to an agreement by providing best practices.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is a suggestion from our former colleague, Assoc Prof Walter Theseira.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A firmer approach is to mandate the installation of charging points in condominiums, as Member Gan Thiam Poh recommended.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: An intermediate approach could be a "Right to Charge" law.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Alternatively, the Government can provide rebates and professional services for installing charging locations within condominiums.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is done in the Canadian province of British Columbia.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There are many things the Government can do.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Senior Parliamentary Secretary clarify what steps are being taken to make progress on this issue?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Since I started my engineering career as an automotive engineer 15 years ago, I have seen many changes in the industry.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It was getting harder and more expensive to do so as we were pushing the limits of science for internal combustion engines, or ICE.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The industry was in a flux as it searched for the right technology platform for the future of transportation.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We tried to squeeze as much energy from each drop of fuel.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We ventured into biodiesel fuels from soya beans and canola which had the effect of increasing the price of this food source instead.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The industry also explored hybrid propulsion systems and hydrogen fuel cells.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There are some who are of the opinion that we in Singapore are not moving fast enough to transit fully into an entirely EV population.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, to transit successfully into an entirely EV population requires more than just technological advancement.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It also requires the right policies and regulations to ensure the safe use of the EVs.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It also necessitates that our infrastructure is adequately prepared to support the EV population.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, while I am supportive of this Bill, I would like to pose a few clarifications for the Senior Parliamentary Secretary.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In addition, we must also consider that other than the traditional automotive manufacturers, more new players are coming into the market; some are not traditional automotive manufacturers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we ensure safety standards are met with each new propulsion system or manufacturer?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To be able to promote and regulate the safe use of EVs, we need to be able to understand these new technologies.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This requires a different skillset from what we have today.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Engineers in regulatory roles will need to understand EVs to ensure their safe use.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There is a need to recruit or upskill/reskill talents in the automotive industry.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Engineers in our LTA need to understand battery technology, safe practices for discharging of batteries and electrical infrastructure to be able to regulate the safe use of these EVs.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, to regulate the safe use of the EVs, our officers must have the right skillset to understand and decide the appropriateness of these new technologies in order to ensure its safe use on our roads.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We need to understand the system, failure rate, redundancy system to understand how it all works so that we can decide on the regulations.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Which system, whose system is safe for use on our roads?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In addition, crashes involving self-driven vehicles or driver-assisted aids, who is to be blamed?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we regulate the insurance of such vehicles?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For development in the braking systems – brake by wire, regenerative braking and driver-assisted braking introduces complexity to the normal hydraulic mechanical brake systems commonly used now.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As they are propelled by electric motors, torque comes instantly at low rpms – and this is known as instant torque.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: An entry level Model 3 Tesla does zero to 100 kilometres per hour in five seconds.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: That is as fast as some high-end performance cars.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Even an entry level city car like the Hyundai Ionic does zero to 100 in 7.7 seconds, which is about twice as quick in acceleration as compared to a Toyota Corolla five years ago.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Tesla Semi Truck, a semi truck that is capable of carrying heavy goods, unladen, can accelerate from zero to 100 in five seconds and the world's fastest production bike accelerates from zero to 100 in two seconds.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, how are we going to be able to keep our roads safe when we will have more of these high-performance vehicles silently plying through our roads?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In addition, how do we manage modifications that are now available for the EVs.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Currently, it is a lot easier to enforce illegal modifications on internal combustion engine cars.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Changing a straight-through exhaust, bigger turbochargers, uprated fuel injectors can be seen by the naked eye.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Not only can the illegal modification be seen, they often can be heard, with frequent complaints to Members of Parliament.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Modifications to the electrical propulsion system though are done through new electronic control units, new software, which are not immediately visually detectable nor can it be heard by our law enforcement officers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Will these modifications increase the risk of battery fires?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What will happen if these battery fires cause a larger fire in a cluster of vehicles at the carpark?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we prevent illegal modifications that make it unsafe for fellow road users?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Imagine our roads becoming more populated with these powerful vehicles that make little or no sound.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, though I am fully supportive of this Bill positioning LTA as the governing body to regulate the safe use of EVs, I would like to caution that this does not represent an incremental change where we can rely solely on the knowledge of the past and our experiences.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: EVs are a disruptive technology that will fundamentally change the automotive industry and we too must be prepared to relook at how we fundamentally manage the safe use of such vehicles.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As it is within the responsibility of LTA to regulate the safe use of these vehicles, it is imperative that the officers in the Ministry are equipped with the right knowledge to address this new technology and be able to approach the policies for the adoption of EVs from a holistic perspective.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There are now a few technical and diploma courses, such as that offered by Singapore Motor Workshop Association Training Academy and Ngee Ann Polytechnic, but more must be done to increase the expertise in these fields in preparation for an entirely EV population.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: One option is to use this as an opportunity to upskill and retrain more individuals from other industries, such as in the aerospace and oil and gas industries, to be proficient in the EV industries.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Beyond safety regulations and enforcement, I am fully supportive of the amendments to the Bill for LTA to cooperate and collaborate with EMA relating to the electrical installation for the charging of EVs.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: By then, what is LTA’s projection of EVs on our roads?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To understand the adequacy of charging stations better, we also need to understand the capability of the charging stations.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How many of the charging stations will be fast charge or slow charge?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Based on the volume and mix of charging stations, is one station for every 16.3 vehicles sufficient?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Based on preliminary assessment on volume and type of charges, do we have enough power in the power grid from clean sources?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Do we need more power stations or substations?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What are the maintenance requirements of these chargers?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Will maintenance be borne by LTA under an umbrella road tax payment or maintenance will be borne by users, in addition to the electricity cost?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Or do we pay a small amount for the charger maintenance or do we pay maintenance through the Town Council on a monthly basis?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How is LTA working closely with MND on the Electrical Load Upgrading (ELU) projects in housing estates?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: When ELU was started in 2014, it was to accommodate the increased electricity consumption in our homes due to the increased use of TVs, PCs, tablets and air-conditioners.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can we ensure that this is done concurrently with the ELU programme in our older estates?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Malay):    EVs are called a disruptive technology.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Therefore, we need to acquire new skillsets to understand how we can use EVs safely.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Besides working with EMA, LTA also needs to work hand in hand with HDB to ensure that the growth of infrastructure matches the growth rate of EVs.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There should be sufficient charging stations to fully support the number of EVs in the near future.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: A clarification is also required on how the usage of such infrastructure will be charged.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Is it through a road tax system that encompasses everything or pay-per-use?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In English): In conclusion, Mdm Deputy Speaker, though EVs pose significant opportunities, we must be aware of the significant changes that they will bring and we must be able to adapt quickly to ensure the safe use of EVs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Taking steps towards a low-carbon future will necessarily involve the uptake of low emission vehicles in Singapore and we are encouraged to see that the Government has safety as their primary concern when it comes to the development of the EV eco-system in Singapore, assuaging the concerns of many Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: When it comes to confronting the ever-advancing technological revolution in Singapore, this is not our taxi drivers' first rodeo.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Before the 1980s, taxis did not even run on digital metres we are now familiar with but had analogue metres hooked up to speedometers that calculated our fares.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In 2006, our taxi drivers had to begin learning how to use the new NETS terminals installed in their vehicles.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Fast forward to today, fares are calculated with algorithms on ride hailing applications, payment transactions are completed virtually without any effort needed by passengers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our taxi drivers have also cooperated with evolving vehicle policies and we have taxi drivers going on diesel, petrol, compressed natural gas (CNG), petrol-electric hybrids and even blue diesel vehicles.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our taxi drivers have seen us through generations of technological advancements, proven capable of relentless adaptation and evolution, and we intend to continue to bring them along for this journey.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, the route that we take in developing our EV eco-system in Singapore will determine whether our taxi drivers can face up to the challenge or will be phased out by the measures taken.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Every policy-maker has two weapons in their arsenal: the carrot and the stick.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is the acumen of and credit to the policy-maker for knowing when to present the carrot and when to brandish the stick.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With the development of an EV eco-system in Singapore and with grand ambitions potentially for EVs to completely replace internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles in Singapore by 2040, I understand the enthusiasm with which we might want to see drivers make the complete switch to electric.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, it must be asked, surely, with 20 years to the finishing line, we certainly do not want our drivers worn out before they get there.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is important that I raise such concerns, with a push for going electric often coming hand in hand with discouragements towards the use of ICE vehicles.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Surely, in decades to come, we will see exorbitant petrol prices as the norm or even zero emission zones out of bounds for ICE vehicles.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But ushering these policies in an over-zealous fashion now will only pile on the troubles for our drivers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Whatever cost we seek to transfer to vehicle owners and drivers in Singapore, they cannot be equally borne by our taxi and private hire drivers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Just as some people cook for a living, some also cook as a hobby.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Should the prices of ingredients shoot up, those who do it as a hobby can and might just stop cooking.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But what is there to do for those who do it as a living?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: If to complement the development of Singapore's EV eco-system, we put in higher barriers for non-taxi and private hire drivers, maybe they will actually think twice about purchasing an ICE vehicle or only drive when it is necessary.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These considerations are, in fact, invalid for point-to-point (P2P) drivers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: If we can promise our taxi and private hire drivers that the onset of EV does not threaten their rice bowl, they will surely support and embrace the new technology.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: After all, our drivers have been very supportive of all our national campaigns and agenda, from getting swabbed to going for vaccinations and being very responsible front-liners supporting Singapore as we emerge from COVID-19.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In addition, for many drivers, their vehicles are optimised for use 24 hours a day with partnerships between day and night drivers or main and relief drivers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How would this impact the existing partnerships between drivers?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How would this impact rental fees and the P2P business model?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The EV eco-system is a complex one with multiple stakeholders and EV is also what we call a two-sided platform.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: There is a need to grow both EVs and charging infrastructure in sync to truly drive adoption.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: As shown in other cities like Beijing, Berlin and London, the public sector plays a key role to get to the inflexion point where the industry has a minimum viable scale to take off, whether it is in mandating subsidies or actually setting up state-owned entities to coordinate the efforts of built charging infrastructure.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: There are many strategies but what is clear is that the public sector plays the key role.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I support the Bill as I believe it will enable Singapore to accelerate the adoption of EVs and catalyse a vibrant EV eco-system while not losing sight of the bigger ambition of moving to a car-lite society.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Notwithstanding, I would like to ask for a few clarifications.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: First, the proposed subsection 4 in section 6 of the Act defines an EV as a vehicle that is propelled wholly or partly by electricity, whether or not it could be self-driving.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Second, the amendment to subsection 1 of section 6 gives LTA the decision rights to set standards for charging devices and equipment in order to protect public safety.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But beyond protecting safety, should there also be a clear vision to take a customer-centred approach to make it seamless for the consumers, including ensuring inter-operability, which will require tight mandates and regulations for grid operators and charging point operators as well as back-end systems that allow facilitation of transactions and adjustments between charge point operators (CPOs) and grid operators?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Third, subsidies have been used in other markets to promote EVs – both demand and supply side subsidies.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Beyond charging infrastructure, investments will also be needed to finance good upgrades as well as land use changes.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Can the Ministry elaborate on how subsidies will play a role in the development of the industry here?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Four, beyond LTA and EMA, many other Government agencies will be involved – such as HDB, URA, to name a few – as well as the private sector.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: One area to pay attention to is the use of data to unlock value not only for the EV market and industry development but also for other national development objectives.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: A robust data framework and a mix of incentives and regulations should also be a key area of focus upfront.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Lastly, in recent years, others in the region, like Indonesia and Thailand, have clinched investments from EV automakers and battery makers – so have we with the Hyundai plant.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Beyond facilitating the establishment of EV and EV charging infrastructure in Singapore, I would like to ask if there are plans to think about EV as a sector to grow and to develop technology and manufacturing capabilities that can be exported.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Notwithstanding the above clarifications, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hence, as much as possible, we should use public transport and continue to invest in a good public transportation system.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe this will not be the only amendment Bill in view of the rapid changes and advancement of technology in the EV sector which is taking place even as we speak.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While we are now looking at the installation of charging stations, there are breakthroughs in battery swapping technology, which can be done within 10 minutes or fewer, as well as fast-charging technology.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Nonetheless, I agree that we cannot afford to wait to see what would be the best charging technology to adopt as we need to proceed with the installation of charging points island-wide.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We need to encourage private investments in the EV charging technology and the use of the latest innovations.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How would the Ministry encourage more local and foreign investments in this industry?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How can we ensure more private investments which can help promote the use of EVs with fast-charging technology and the building of multiple charging points from a single source in all our public and private carparks?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As the prices of EVs come down, they will provide an equally attractive, if not cheaper and cost-effective mode of transport.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The eradication of carbon emissions and thus less need for maintenance are additional advantages.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How would the Ministry ensure standard adoption and enforcement of safety measures?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have some concerns about the additional demands on our power grid and, in a way, a loss of diversification in terms of energy sourcing for vehicles.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the unfortunate event of a blackout, presently, most vehicles can continue to move around on our roads since they are powered by petrol and diesel.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When most cars are powered by electricity, the impact of a blackout will be much heavier.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Ministry share with us how we can prevent and mitigate the impact of such an event?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They should not be another waste to contaminate our fragile planet.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: They have also raised issues on EV charger regulation and other EV-related topics, which are important as EVs become increasingly common.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: To clarify, for the purposes of this Bill, the definition of EV includes battery electric vehicles and plug-in hybrid vehicles but excludes other types of hybrid vehicles that cannot be recharged by plugging in to an external source of electrical power.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: Safety must be of priority in all aspects of EV use and charging.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: That is why we abide by stringent safety standards.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: For example, LTA mandates that the electric powertrain of EVs must meet requirements in the United Nations Economic Commission for Europe Regulations.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: For software that governs EV performance, such as motor power output and batteries, we will need to work with EV manufacturers to explore ways to guard against illegal modifications.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: EV charging systems are governed by Technical Reference 25, or TR25, which is based on global standards set by organisations like the International Electrotechnical Commission.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: TR25 is tailored to our warm and humid weather conditions and guards against safety hazards like overheating or electrocution.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: Every review of TR25 is a consultative process involving industry stakeholders, academics and Government agencies.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: This ensures that TR25 supports innovation in EV charging technology, while ensuring public safety.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: Licensed electrical workers are required to ensure, and only install, EV chargers that are TR25 compliant.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: It is an offence under the Electricity Act to tamper with electrical installations, which include fixed EV chargers.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat can be assured that these requirements will remain in place, regardless of the agency in charge of regulating EV chargers.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: Mr Louis Ng asked about the Ministry's plans to promote adoption of electric motorcycles.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: As he pointed out, there are some barriers to electric motorcycle adoption today that are beyond our control.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: Globally, there are not many electric motorcycle models, compared to electric cars.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: Many motorcycle dealers and distributors have also not adjusted to the electric motorcycle market yet.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: Therefore, we have not included motorcycles in our 2030 cleaner energy target on new registrations at the moment.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: As the global market for electric motorcycle matures, we should see more offerings for consumers.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: We will continue to monitor such trends and consider suitable measures to encourage adoption if necessary.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: At the same time, we will look into providing for the charging needs of vehicles like electric motorcycles and goods vehicles, as part of our charger deployment plans.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: We will also not rule out battery swapping for motorcycles.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: Third, on available grid capacity to support EVs.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: EMA and LTA are working with local researchers to study the long-term electrical infrastructure needs for EV charging in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
